This manifests concretely when the training batch size is small relative to class diversity — with batch size 64 across 1000 ImageNet classes, each batch samples a tiny relational neighborhood, and the student's encoder is penalized for any deviation from the teacher's pairwise distances within that neighborhood, effectively learning a distorted metric that overfits to frequently co-occurring sample pairs rather than class-level geometry. Park and Kim (2019) noted that RKD with distance-wise loss degraded on fine-grained retrieval benchmarks relative to angle-wise loss, which is consistent with this mechanism: distance magnitudes are more batch-sensitive than angular structure, so distance-wise RKD induces stronger relational overfitting. A second and distinct pathology arises under semantic asymmetry between teacher and student capacity: the teacher's relational structure encodes high-order feature interactions that require its full representational dimensionality to be geometrically consistent, but when the student reproduces this structure in a lower-dimensional space it must introduce metric distortions — analogous to the impossibility of isometrically embedding a high-dimensional manifold into a lower-dimensional one — and these distortions systematically compress inter-class margins for semantically similar classes, precisely the pairs that matter most for generalization. Tian et al. (2020) in CRD (Contrastive Representation Distillation) showed that contrastive relational objectives outperformed RKD on transfer benchmarks, but their method is vulnerable to a third pathology: false negative contamination, where semantically similar samples treated as negatives in the contrastive loss push apart representations that should be geometrically close, creating a student embedding space with artificially inflated inter-class distances that collapse under distribution shift when the false negative structure changes.
